newsitem.title: CHINA: Caterpillar says China venture sales, losses lower.
newsitem.headline: Caterpillar says China venture sales, losses lower.

text.p: Caterpillar Inc's troubled Shanghai diesel engine joint venture saw lower sales last year than expected due to a weak market, but losses were also below planned levels, a company official said.

John Airola, director of Caterpillar's Shanghai operation, said in an interview there were signs of an upturn in sales from the joint venture, 55 percent owned by Caterpillar and 45 percent by Shanghai Diesel Engine Co Ltd
"Sales were lower than expected (in 1996), but from an overall profit perspective, we are on track," Airola said. "The losses were lower than expected due to cost containment measures."
But I think we've seen the bottom. There are signs of increased sales," he added.
Airola declined to give figures for sales volume, revenue or the losses so far for the $29 million joint venture, CAT Shanghai Engine Co Ltd, which started production in early 1995.

A spokesman for Shanghai Diesel on Wednesday agreed that 1996 sales for the joint venture firm were not good. He declined to give details beyond saying that sales totalled less than 200 engines for the year.

"Shanghai Diesel officials told us in February they wanted to look at closing down the joint venture, but the government has urged them to continue because it is a very high-profile project," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai.
Caterpillar's Airola said he did not currently see any prospect of changes in the setup.
"We continue to talk, which is the way things should be," he said.
Diesel officials have previously indicated the joint venture lost 31 million yuan in 1995, selling only 160 engines for the construction industry against an original plan of 500.
One of Shanghai Diesel's complaints has been the low level of local content sourcing for the six-cylinder diesel engines produced by the joint venture firm.
"The main problem is that costs are too high, about one-third higher than the cost of most China-produced engines," the Shanghai Diesel spokesman said.
"To deal with this we are talking to Caterpillar about localising content as fast as possible," he added.
Airola said local content was currently about 10 percent but was expected to rise to 60 percent by the end of 1998.
"The localisation schedule is behind," he said. "It's the issue of meeting world class quality standards."
Shanghai Diesel is the largest potential supplier of local components.
Another analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai said he felt part of the problem was Caterpillar's approach to the China market.
"It appears the Caterpillar people are serious about producing engines to the same level of quality they produce in the United States, whereas the Chinese market prefers cost over quality," he said.
Airola said the low sales volumes were exacerbating the venture's problem, which gave the company and its suppliers less of an opportunity to raise quality.
"The higher the volume, the more you learn and the faster you improve," he said.
